tea:bhagavad-gita:1.28.title: Bhagavad Gītā
tea:bhagavad-gita:1.28.original:

tea:bhagavad-gita:2.7.title: Bhagavad Gītā
tea:bhagavad-gita:2.7.original:
kārpaṇyadoṣopahatasvabhāvaḥ
pṛcchāmi tvāṃ dharmasaṃmūḍhacetāḥ|
yacchreyaḥ syānniśicataṃ brūhi tanme
śiṣyaste'haṃ śādhi māṃ tvāṃ prapannam
tea:bhagavad-gita:2.7.paraphrase: Arjuna: my very nature struck by the fault of pitiable weakness (kārpaṇya-doṣa), my mind bewildered about dharma (dharma-saṃmūḍha-cetāḥ), I ask you: tell me decisively what is better (śreyas). I am your disciple (śiṣya); instruct me, who have taken refuge in you (tvāṃ prapannam).

tea:satipatthana-sutta:mn10:2.title: Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta
tea:satipatthana-sutta:mn10:2.original: “Ekāyano ayaṁ, bhikkhave, maggo sattānaṁ visuddhiyā, sokaparidevānaṁ samatikkamāya, dukkhadomanassānaṁ atthaṅgamāya, ñāyassa adhigamāya, nibbānassa sacchikiriyāya, yadidaṁ cattāro satipaṭṭhānā.
tea:satipatthana-sutta:mn10:2.paraphrase: The Buddha declares that this is a one-way path (ekāyana maggo) for the purification of beings, for overcoming sorrow and lamentation (soka-parideva), for the ending of pain and displeasure (dukkha-domanassa), for reaching the right method (ñāya), and for realising nibbāna: namely, the four satipaṭṭhānas (establishments of mindfulness).

tea:tattvartha-sutra:9.28.title: Tattvārthasūtra
tea:tattvartha-sutra:9.28.paraphrase: Dhyāna is of four kinds: ārta (pained), raudra (fierce), dharmya (of dharma) and śukla (white).

tea:tattvartha-sutra:9.29.title: Tattvārthasūtra
tea:tattvartha-sutra:9.29.paraphrase: The latter two [dharmya and śukla] are the causes (hetu) of liberation (mokṣa).

tea:tattvartha-sutra:9.30.title: Tattvārthasūtra
tea:tattvartha-sutra:9.30.paraphrase: Ārta [dhyāna] is a continuous bringing to mind (smṛti-samanvāhāra) directed at separation from a disagreeable (amanojña) thing when one is in contact with it.

tea:tattvartha-sutra:9.31.title: Tattvārthasūtra
tea:tattvartha-sutra:9.31.paraphrase: The reverse, in the case of the agreeable (manojña).

tea:tattvartha-sutra:9.32.title: Tattvārthasūtra
tea:tattvartha-sutra:9.32.paraphrase: And [ārta dhyāna is also] in the case of feeling (vedanā).

tea:tattvartha-sutra:9.7.title: Tattvārthasūtra
tea:tattvartha-sutra:9.7.paraphrase: The anuprekṣās (repeated contemplations) are anucintana of: impermanence (anitya), no refuge (aśaraṇa), the round of births (saṃsāra), aloneness (ekatva), otherness (anyatva), impurity (aśuci), inflow (āsrava), stopping (saṃvara), shedding (nirjarā), the universe (loka), the rarity of enlightenment (bodhi-durlabha), and the well-taught nature of dharma (dharma-svākhyātatva).

tea:yoga-bhasya:1.31.title: Yogabhāṣya (Vyāsa's commentary on the Yoga Sūtra)
tea:yoga-bhasya:1.31.original:
duḥkham ādhyātmikam ādhibhautikam ādhidaivikaṃ ca /
yenābhihatāḥ prāṇinas tadapaghātāya prayatante tad duḥkham /
daurmanasyam icchāvighātāc cetasaḥ kṣobhaḥ /
yad aṅgāny ejayati kampayati tad aṅgamejayatvam /
prāṇo yad bāhyaṃ vāyum ācāmati sa śvāsaḥ /
yat kauṣṭhyaṃ vāyuṃ niḥsārayati sa praśvāsaḥ /
ete vikṣepasahabhuvo vikṣiptacittasyaite bhavanti /
samāhitacittasyaite na bhavanti
tea:yoga-bhasya:1.31.paraphrase: Pain (duḥkha) is of three kinds: relating to oneself (ādhyātmika), to other beings (ādhibhautika), and to the divine (ādhidaivika); it is that by which beings are struck and strive to strike it down. Dejection (daurmanasya) is a disturbance (kṣobha) of the mind through the frustration of a wish. Trembling of the limbs (aṅgamejayatva) is that which shakes the limbs. Inhalation (śvāsa) is when the vital breath (prāṇa) takes in outer air; exhalation (praśvāsa) is when it expels air from the belly. These are companions of distraction: they occur in one whose mind is distracted (vikṣipta); they do not occur in one whose mind is concentrated (samāhita).

tea:yoga-sutra:1.31.title: Yoga Sūtra of Patañjali
tea:yoga-sutra:1.31.paraphrase: Pain (duḥkha), dejection (daurmanasya), trembling of the limbs (aṅgamejayatva), and inhalation and exhalation (śvāsa, praśvāsa) accompany the distractions.

summary: You described a pattern that the texts name: Ārta-dhyāna (sorrowful dwelling), in the Jain texts. It is shown below with your own words and the texts' description.

points.text: The Vedic and yogic texts have their own account of a pattern like the one above: Daurmanasya (dejection) (a partial match for Ārta-dhyāna (sorrowful dwelling)). Dejection is agitation of the mind from the thwarting of a wish (icchā-vighāta). Your words were matched to Ārta-dhyāna (sorrowful dwelling), not to this; it is shown so that both readings are in view.

Your words “i want to go straight back to it” fit only loosely what the Jain texts call Ārta-dhyāna (sorrowful dwelling). Meditation (dhyāna) is of four kinds: sorrowful (ārta), cruel (raudra), virtuous (dharmya) and pure (śukla) (TS 9.28); the last two are causes of liberation (TS 9.29).

Your words “i want to go straight back to it” were matched to Ārta-dhyāna (sorrowful dwelling). Across the traditions: Each names a sinking, sorrowful turn of mind. Vyāsa: dejection (daurmanasya) is a disturbance of the mind through the frustration of a wish, and it accompanies distraction (YS 1.31; YB 1.31). Gītā: Arjuna is overcome by pity and despairing (viṣīdan), his mind bewildered about dharma (BhG 1.28, 2.1, 2.7). TS: sorrowful dwelling (ārta-dhyāna) dwells on removing the disagreeable, on keeping the agreeable, on pain, and on longing for future enjoyment (TS 9.30–33). MN 10 declares the four establishments of mindfulness a path to the ending of pain and displeasure (dukkha-domanassa) (MN 10:2). Under the one-truth principle, they describe it from different standpoints: the match is a partial match, not an identity.

differences.text: Your words “i want to go straight back to it” were matched to Ārta-dhyāna (sorrowful dwelling). Across the traditions: (1) Daurmanasya in YS is a companion of distraction: it occurs in a distracted mind and is absent in a concentrated one (YB 1.31). (2) Arjuna's viṣāda is a crisis about dharma, and it becomes the occasion of the whole teaching (BhG 2.7). (3) Jain ārta-dhyāna is a kind of meditation (dhyāna), the inauspicious sorrowful one of four (TS 9.28): a sustained fixing of the mind, not a passing mood. This row describes states the texts name. It is not a finding about any person, and it makes no health claim.
